description: Why markets sometimes fail — public goods, merit and demerit goods, and under- or over-provision of resources.
content_html:
When Markets Get It Wrong

Markets are powerful. When they work well, the price mechanism allocates scarce resources efficiently — firms produce what consumers want, at prices that reflect costs and value. But markets are not perfect. Sometimes the price mechanism produces an outcome that is not best for society as a whole. Economists call this market failure. It is one of the most important reasons why governments intervene in the economy.

Market failure leads to a misallocation of resources. That means society ends up with too much of some things (goods that cause harm) and too little of others (goods that bring wide benefits). Understanding why this happens is the first step to understanding what government can do about it.

Key Fact

Market failure occurs when the free market, left to itself, produces a socially inefficient outcome — either too little of a beneficial good (under-provision) or too much of a harmful one (over-provision).

Public Goods: The Free-Rider Problem

Some goods have two special properties that make it impossible for private firms to profit from selling them. Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival. Take national defence: once the armed forces protect a country, every person in that country benefits — you cannot protect some citizens and leave others undefended, and one person being protected does not make anyone else less protected.

Because you cannot exclude anyone from consuming a public good, private firms cannot charge a price for it. If a firm tried to sell flood defence, every household near a river would benefit whether they paid or not. Those who do not pay are called free-riders. Since every rational consumer has an incentive to free-ride, no firm can make a profit, and the good will not be provided at all by the private market. This is a clear market failure: society needs the good but the market will not supply it.

Non-excludable means it is impossible (or prohibitively expensive) to stop someone from consuming the good once it is provided. A lighthouse beam shining across the sea cannot be switched off for ships that did not pay the lighthouse keeper.

Non-rival means one person consuming the good does not reduce the amount available to anyone else. If you watch a firework display, you do not ‘use up’ any of the fireworks for the family standing next to you.

A pure public good has both properties simultaneously. Examples include national defence, street lighting and flood barriers. Most goods are private goods — excludable (you need a ticket) and rival (a seat taken by one person cannot be taken by another). Some goods fall in between, such as a congested road (non-excludable but now rival when full).

Merit Goods: Under-Consumed by the Market

Merit goods are goods that are good for you — but consumers tend to underestimate just how good. Education and healthcare are the classic examples. A teenager who drops out of school may not fully appreciate the lifetime earnings they are giving up, nor the wider benefits their skills would bring to employers, taxpayers and the broader economy. Because individuals undervalue these goods, they consume less of them than would be best for society. The free market, responding only to what people are willing to pay, therefore under-provides merit goods.

This is a form of information failure. People do not make perfectly informed decisions. A young person might not know the long-run return on investing in education. A patient might underestimate the future value of a vaccination that protects not just themselves but everyone they interact with. Because the private benefit is underestimated, demand is too low and the free market produces less than the socially optimal quantity.

Key Fact

Merit goods (such as education, healthcare and vaccinations) are under-consumed by the free market because consumers underestimate their true benefits. The result is under-provision: society ends up with less of these goods than would be socially efficient.

Demerit Goods: Over-Consumed by the Market

Demerit goods are the mirror image of merit goods. They are goods where the true costs — to the individual and to society — are greater than consumers appreciate. Cigarettes, alcohol and illegal drugs are the most cited examples. A smoker pays for the cigarettes they buy, but they do not fully account for the long-run harm to their own health, or the costs imposed on the NHS, on family members, and on employers through lost productivity.

Because consumers underestimate the true cost, they buy more than is socially optimal. Private firms are happy to sell as much as consumers demand. The result is over-provision: the free market produces and sells too much of these goods. Society bears costs — in the form of healthcare bills, lost working days and social harm — that are not reflected in the market price. This gap between the price paid and the true social cost is at the heart of the market failure.

The confusion between merit and demerit goods is a very common error. The key is to focus on the direction of the information failure and the direction of the problem it creates.

Merit goods: benefits are underestimated → demand is too low → the free market under-provides → government may subsidise or provide directly (e.g. the NHS, free schooling).

Demerit goods: costs are underestimated → demand is too high → the free market over-provides → government may tax or regulate (e.g. tobacco duty, age restrictions on alcohol).

Both arise from information failure — the consumer does not have full or accurate knowledge about the true benefit or true cost of the good.

Information Failure and Resource Misallocation

Information failure is the common thread running through merit and demerit goods. When buyers or sellers lack full information, prices do not accurately signal the true social value of a good, and resources flow to the wrong places. Consider a market for private health insurance: a consumer with a hidden medical condition knows more about their own health risk than the insurer does. The insurer cannot price the policy accurately. This information gap distorts the market and can cause it to fail entirely.

The result of all these failures — public goods not provided, merit goods under-consumed, demerit goods over-consumed — is a misallocation of resources. Society would be better off if it produced more healthcare and education, less tobacco and alcohol, and had effective national defence and street lighting. But the free market, responding only to price signals and private incentives, cannot always deliver this. It is here that the argument for government intervention begins.

Governments have several tools to tackle misallocation. For public goods, the most straightforward response is direct state provision — the government funds and provides the good itself (for example, funding the armed forces through taxation). For merit goods, governments may use subsidies to lower the price and encourage greater consumption, or provide the good free at the point of use (as with the NHS). For demerit goods, governments can impose taxes to raise the price and deter consumption — tobacco duty is the classic example. Regulation (such as minimum age limits or advertising bans) is another tool. You will look at all of these in detail in a later lesson on government intervention.
exam_tip_html: Questions on market failure often use the command word ‘explain’ or ‘analyse’. For an Explain question (3 or 4 marks), identify the type of market failure clearly (public good, merit good, demerit good or information failure), then develop a chain: what the consumer does, why that is different from the socially optimal outcome, and what the result is for resource allocation. For an Analyse or Evaluate question, always distinguish between why the market fails and how government might respond — and then question whether the intervention actually works. A common error is confusing under-provision (merit goods — market produces too little) with over-provision (demerit goods — market produces too much). Get the direction of the failure right before you begin.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Market failure occurs when the free market misallocates resources, producing too little of some goods and too much of others. The main causes are public goods, merit goods, demerit goods and information failure.
  • Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival; the free-rider problem means no private firm will supply them, so the government must. Merit goods are under-consumed because benefits are underestimated; demerit goods are over-consumed because costs are underestimated.
  • Information failure is the root cause of merit and demerit good market failure. Government tools to correct misallocation include direct provision, subsidies, taxes and regulation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a public good?
A) A cinema ticket
B) A cup of coffee from a café
C) Street lighting
D) A gym membership
practice_questions.marks: C) Street lighting [1 mark]. Street lighting is non-excludable (you cannot stop passers-by from using it) and non-rival (one person benefiting does not reduce the light available to others). The other options are private goods that are both excludable and rival.

practice_questions.text: A local council is considering whether to provide a firework display on New Year's Eve. Using your knowledge of public goods, explain why a private firm is unlikely to provide this display.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a firework display is non-excludable (people nearby can watch without paying) and/or non-rival (one person watching does not reduce others' enjoyment); 1 mark for linking this to the free-rider problem: since the firm cannot charge all beneficiaries, it cannot cover its costs, so no profit-maximising firm would supply it.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the free market tends to under-provide merit goods.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying merit goods as goods whose benefits are underestimated by consumers (information failure); 1 mark for explaining that because consumers undervalue the good, demand is lower than the socially optimal level; 1 mark for concluding that the market therefore produces less than society needs, resulting in under-provision. Example: individuals may under-invest in further education because they do not fully appreciate the long-run earnings benefit, so without intervention the market provides too few university places.

practice_questions.text: A government is concerned that cigarette consumption is causing significant harm to public health. Explain, using the concept of demerit goods, why the free market leads to over-consumption of cigarettes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining demerit goods as goods whose true costs are greater than consumers realise; 1 mark for explaining that consumers underestimate the long-run health costs of smoking (information failure); 1 mark for explaining that because the full cost is not reflected in the market price, consumers demand more than is socially optimal; 1 mark for concluding that the result is over-provision — more cigarettes are produced and consumed than society would choose if fully informed, leading to a misallocation of resources (too many resources in tobacco production, too few elsewhere).

practice_questions.text: A national economy has a large number of people who do not complete secondary education. Analyse how this could be linked to the market failure of information failure and the under-provision of merit goods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear and sustained chain of reasoning from information failure through to resource misallocation. Identifies that education is a merit good whose benefits (higher lifetime earnings, productivity gains for the wider economy, social benefits such as lower crime) are underestimated by young people and their families. Links this to the mechanism: because demand is based on perceived rather than true benefit, market demand is below the socially optimal level; a free-market school system would set fees, further depressing demand among lower-income groups; outcome is under-provision relative to what maximises social welfare. Chain developed with specific cause-and-effect logic.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies education as a merit good and explains under-consumption due to information failure. Explains under-provision but chain may be incomplete or lack the social/external benefit dimension.

Developing (2 marks): States that education is a merit good and people do not consume enough, but explanation is limited or incomplete.

Emerging (1 mark): Simple point about markets not providing enough education, with little or no development.

practice_questions.text:
'Government provision is the most effective way to correct the market failure associated with public goods.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival, so the free-rider problem means no private firm will provide them profitably; direct government provision (funded through taxation) solves this by removing the need for a market price.
- Examples such as national defence, the police service and street lighting show that state provision can deliver public goods effectively and universally.
- Without government provision, society would have none of these goods at all — the market failure would be total.
- Government can ensure the good is provided at the socially optimal level rather than at zero (market outcome).

Arguments against / limitations:
- Government provision is not costless — it must be funded through taxation, which can create its own distortions and disincentives.
- Government may not know the socially optimal quantity and could over- or under-provide; this is known as government failure.
- Some goods that look like public goods can be made partially excludable with technology (e.g. toll roads, pay-per-view broadcasts), allowing private provision in some circumstances.
- For merit and demerit goods, government provision is not always the best tool; subsidies, taxes or regulation may be more efficient and less expensive.
- Political pressures may cause government to over-provide (to win votes) or under-provide (to cut spending), rather than reaching the socially efficient level.

Conclusion (supported judgement required):
- Government provision is arguably the only solution that fully resolves public good market failure, since the non-excludability property rules out private supply. However, its effectiveness depends on whether the government can accurately identify the socially optimal level and avoid the costs of government failure. The judgement depends on the specific good, the efficiency of public administration in that country, and whether alternative tools (technology or partial charges) are available.

Mastering (10–12 marks): Sophisticated two-sided argument, analysis of both the case for and significant limitations of government provision, supported judgement that weighs the strength of the arguments (e.g. ‘it depends on’ the nature of the good and the risk of government failure).

Secure (7–9 marks): Clear two-sided argument with explanation of why government provision addresses the free-rider problem, plus at least one developed counter-argument. Conclusion present but may lack full support.

Developing (4–6 marks): Some two-sided analysis but limited development on one side; conclusion may be weak or unsupported.

Emerging (1–3 marks): One-sided or mostly descriptive response; limited understanding of public goods or government failure.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a public good?
options: A good sold by the government at a subsidised price
A good that is non-excludable and non-rival
A good that benefits society more than individuals realise
A good that is harmful to consumers but produced in large quantities

knowledge_checks.q: Why does the free market tend to over-provide demerit goods?
options: Because demerit goods are cheaper to produce than other goods
Because the government subsidises demerit goods to keep prices low
Because consumers underestimate the true costs of demerit goods and so demand more than is socially optimal
Because demerit goods are non-excludable, so firms cannot charge for them

knowledge_checks.q: People who benefit from a public good without paying for it are known as _____.
Merit goods are under-consumed by the free market because consumers experience _____, meaning they do not fully appreciate the true benefits.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Non-excludable and non-rival; the free market will not provide it
Under-consumed because its benefits are underestimated by consumers
Over-consumed because its costs are underestimated by consumers

flashcard_questions.a: When the free market misallocates resources, producing a socially inefficient outcome.

flashcard_questions.q: What two properties define a public good?

flashcard_questions.a: When people benefit from a good without paying, making private provision unprofitable.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two examples of public goods.

flashcard_questions.a: A good whose benefits are underestimated by consumers, leading to under-consumption.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the free market under-provide merit goods?
flashcard_questions.a: Consumers undervalue the benefits, so market demand is below the socially optimal level.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two examples of merit goods.

flashcard_questions.a: A good whose costs are underestimated by consumers, leading to over-consumption.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the free market over-provide demerit goods?
flashcard_questions.a: Consumers underestimate the true costs, so demand exceeds the socially optimal quantity.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two examples of demerit goods.
What is information failure in economics?
flashcard_questions.a: When buyers or sellers lack full knowledge of true costs or benefits, distorting market decisions.

flashcard_questions.q: Merit goods lead to ___-provision; demerit goods lead to ___-provision by the free market.
What tool might a government use to correct under-provision of a merit good?
flashcard_questions.a: A subsidy to lower the price, or direct provision free at the point of use.

flashcard_questions.q: Why will no private firm supply a pure public good?
flashcard_questions.a: Non-excludability means free-riders cannot be charged, so no profit can be made.

glossary_terms.definition: The failure of the free market to allocate resources efficiently, leading to an outcome that is not socially optimal.
A situation in which resources are not used in the most efficient way, meaning too much of some goods is produced and too little of others.
A good that is non-excludable (you cannot stop people from using it) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce what is available to others).
People who benefit from a good or service without paying for it, because they cannot be excluded from its consumption.
A good or service that brings greater benefits to individuals and society than consumers realise, leading to under-consumption if left to the free market.
A good or service that is more harmful to individuals and society than consumers realise, leading to over-consumption if left to the free market.
A type of market failure where consumers lack full knowledge about the true costs or benefits of a good, causing them to make decisions that are not in their best interest.
